text: Our office espresso machine is leaking. A wants a simpler one and B wants to keep the old one. I don't want a fight over coffee. Can you help us sort it out?

Hi A — C asked me to facilitate a conversation about the office espresso machine (it's leaking) and the grinder. I'm not here to push a solution or take sides; my job is to gather what matters to each of you and keep a list everyone can see.

So to start: what matters to you about the espresso machine and grinder, and why? What's your worry if things go one way or the other? I'm just as interested in small or practical things as big ones — and if you'd rather not share something, that's fine too. I won't treat anything as settled until you tell me I've got it right.

I’d like us to have coffee equipment that’s reliable and doesn’t need much upkeep; we all use it every day, and the leak is worrying. I know the old machine means a lot to B, so I wouldn’t want that to be brushed aside. I’m also a little concerned about ending up with repairs, a cleaning rota, or lots of ongoing decisions—I’m pretty worn out after work. The grinder matters too, though I’m not sure yet what the best option is for it.

Hi B — C asked me to facilitate a conversation about the office espresso machine (it's leaking) and the grinder. I'm not here to push a solution or take sides; my job is to gather what matters to each of you and keep a list everyone can see.

I want the old machine repaired and kept, with its grinder. It’s ours—A’s and mine—and it belonged to our late father, so replacing it feels like throwing away more than a machine. But it keeps breaking, and I don’t have much time for a drawn-out repair or debate. My worry is either losing something important to us or getting stuck maintaining it forever.

Thanks for reaching out, C. I'm happy to help — I'll facilitate and keep a shared list of concerns.

You mentioned A wants a simpler machine and B wants to keep the old one, and that you don't want a fight over coffee. I'd like to hear yours as your own concern, not just as the go-between: what matters to you about the espresso machine and grinder situation, and why? What would make this feel handled well for you? Even small or practical things count.
I’d like us to have working coffee again, without this turning into a fight. I don’t have a preference about which machine we use, and I can’t take on coordinating the repair or decision myself.

Thanks A — here's what I've got from you, put positively and without naming any particular outcome. Please tell me if it fits, or fix my wording:

1. Coffee equipment that's dependable and easy to keep going — and that doesn't turn into a job or a stream of ongoing decisions for you.
2. That what the old machine means to B doesn't get brushed aside.

(Your point about the grinder being unresolved is noted — I'll come back to it.)

Shared list so far:
1. A — dependable, low-effort coffee equipment, not a job or a stream of decisions.
2. B — keeping the old machine and grinder, which carry family meaning, in use, without endless repairs or a long process.
3. C — working coffee again, no fight, without C running the repair or the decision.
4. A — that B's attachment to the old machine isn't brushed aside.

Do 1 and 2 fit you? Anything missing, even small?
Yes, those fit. I’d add that I want coffee to be reliably available for everyday use, without taking on repairs or ongoing upkeep myself.

Thanks B — here's what I've got from you, put positively and without naming any particular outcome. Please tell me if it fits, or fix my wording:

1. That the machine and grinder your dad left you and A stay in your lives and in use — the meaning of them isn't thrown away.
2. That this doesn't become drawn out: no prolonged repair saga or debate, and no being the one stuck maintaining it forever.

That fits, and I've folded it in. Updated list (same numbers, entries 1 and 3 revised, 6 added):

1. A — coffee reliably available for everyday use, on dependable, low-effort equipment, without A taking on repairs or ongoing upkeep.
2. B — Dad's machine kept in use (not the grinder as an heirloom); its meaning isn't thrown away.
3. B — no drawn-out repair or debate; any work fits small chunks of B's time; no hard deadline.
4. C — working coffee again, no fight.
5. C — not C coordinating the repair or the decision.
6. A — B's attachment to the old machine isn't brushed aside.

Now some options meant to meet all six. Nothing is decided — tell me which ones work for you and, importantly, does anyone have even a minor discomfort with any of them?

O1. Keep the old machine and its grinder; get it repaired by a technician in as few visits as possible, booked and paid for through the office (facilities/office manager handles it, not A or C). Ask the technician to set it up so routine care is minimal, and have a note on the machine saying who to tell if it leaks.
O2. Same as O1, plus a modest backup: a simple low-maintenance machine alongside it, so everyday coffee doesn't depend on the old one, which stays in use for whoever wants it.
O3. Repair the old machine and keep it in use as the everyday machine, with the grinder kept matched to it; any further problem gets one scheduled service call rather than an open-ended project.

I can't spend or commit money myself — these are shapes for you all to agree on. Which feel right, and any small discomfort?

O2 feels closest: dependable everyday coffee without putting the old machine’s meaning aside. I’m a little uneasy about O1 and O3 making the repaired machine central, given the leak. I’d also want it clear that any upkeep is handled by the office, not added to my plate.
